Gas Safety Procedure

Supersedes the version effective 1 September 2024. Internal escalation contact changed from the Facilities Lead to the new 24-hour Estates Helpdesk.

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how staff respond to a suspected gas leak at any Alderbridge site. It applies to every member of staff on shift.

Policy statement

A suspected gas leak is treated as an immediate, serious hazard, evacuated and reported without delay, since gas presents a risk that can escalate very quickly if not acted on immediately.

Definitions

**Suspected gas leak** the smell of gas, a hissing sound near a gas appliance or pipe, or any other sign suggesting a gas leak. **National Gas Emergency Service** the national emergency number for a suspected gas leak, called immediately in every case. **24-hour Estates Helpdesk** the new internal contact notified after the emergency call, replacing the previous direct line to the Facilities Lead, staffed around the clock including out of hours.

Evacuate the immediate area on any suspected gas leak, moving residents and staff to a safe distance.

Do not operate a light switch, or any other electrical switch, in the affected area, since a spark can ignite escaping gas.

Call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999 immediately, giving a clear description of the location and what has been noticed.

Notify the 24-hour Estates Helpdesk once the emergency call has been made; this has replaced the previous direct line to the Facilities Lead, particularly improving out-of-hours coverage.

Do not re-enter the affected area until the National Gas Emergency Service or a qualified engineer confirms it is safe.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a suspected leak is very minor and localised (for example, a faint smell near a single appliance) staff still evacuate that immediate area and call the National Gas Emergency Service; the procedure is never scaled down based on an initial impression that the leak seems small.

Outbreak Management Procedure

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group declares, manages and closes an infectious disease outbreak at any of its sites. It applies to every site and covers respiratory, gastrointestinal and other transmissible infections, working alongside the wider infection prevention and control framework the Hand Hygiene Policy and PPE Guidance establish for everyday practice.

Policy statement

An outbreak in a communal care setting spreads faster and affects more vulnerable people than in almost any other environment, and Alderbridge treats early, decisive action as protecting residents' health first and their normal social and family life second — never the reverse, but also never sustaining a restriction for longer than the evidence genuinely requires.

Definitions

**Outbreak** two or more people supported or staff at the same site developing symptoms of the same suspected infection within 48 hours. **Incubation period** the time between exposure to an infectious agent and the appearance of symptoms, used to determine how long an outbreak's control measures must continue after the last new case. **Enhanced cleaning** an increased frequency and intensity of cleaning specific to the suspected pathogen, beyond the site's everyday standard. **Cohorting** grouping affected and unaffected people, and where practicable staff, separately to limit further transmission.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** declares an outbreak, notifies the local Health Protection Team and the Alderbridge Quality Lead, and leads the site's own outbreak response. **Every member of staff** reports any new suspected case immediately and follows the enhanced cleaning and PPE requirements without exception once an outbreak is declared. **The Alderbridge Quality Lead** coordinates any cross-site implication (for example, a staff member who has worked shifts at two sites during the incubation period) and reports outbreak activity to the Board.

On identifying a second case of the same suspected infection within 48 hours of the first, the registered manager declares an outbreak and notifies the local Health Protection Team the same day.

Use the outbreak decision tree appendix when uncertain whether a situation meets the outbreak trigger.

Support antimicrobial stewardship by providing the GP with clear, accurate observation of a resident's symptoms rather than requesting antibiotic treatment proactively; this new section is introduced in this version.

Follow the Outbreak Management Procedure's enhanced precautions once an outbreak is confirmed.

Why antimicrobial stewardship was added

Sector-wide guidance increasingly emphasises the role every care provider plays in reducing unnecessary antibiotic use, since antimicrobial resistance is a genuine, growing risk to everyone's future treatment options; Alderbridge's own contribution is to observe accurately and support the GP's clinical decision rather than push for antibiotic treatment as a default response to every infection concern.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a resident's condition appears to be deteriorating rapidly, staff still escalate for an urgent clinical review immediately; antimicrobial stewardship is about appropriate, evidence-based use, never about delaying a genuinely urgent clinical response.

A site experiencing a higher-than-average infection incidence receives additional Infection Prevention and Control Lead support and more frequent local audit.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This manual sits above the Hand Hygiene Policy, Personal Protective Equipment Guidance, Clinical Waste Procedure, Laundry Management Procedure and Outbreak Management Procedure, now also introducing the stewardship principle referenced in the Medication Management Manual's own PRN and general prescribing guidance.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates a real outbreak response. Two residents at Meadow Court develop diarrhoea and vomiting within a day of each other. The registered manager declares an outbreak, notifies the Health Protection Team, and begins enhanced cleaning with a chlorine-based disinfectant per their advice. A third and fourth case follow over the next two days, all cohorted in one wing with dedicated staff. No new case occurs after day 5, and the outbreak is declared over on day 7 (2 incubation periods of roughly 48 hours each, plus a safety margin) following confirmation with the Health Protection Team, at which point normal visiting and communal activity resume.

Frequently asked questions

**Can a visiting family member refuse to follow an outbreak-related restriction?** The restriction is explained clearly and applied consistently to protect everyone at the site; a family member who does not accept it is asked not to visit during the outbreak period, escalated to the registered manager if needed. **Does an outbreak declaration have to be reported to the CQC?** Where it meets the CQC Notification Procedure's own threshold (for example, a significant impact on service delivery), yes; the registered manager checks this alongside the Health Protection Team notification, not instead of it. **What if staff themselves are affected in large enough numbers to threaten safe staffing?** The Business Continuity Plan Summary's cross-site resource-sharing arrangement is considered, alongside agency support if genuinely needed.

Training and competency

Registered managers and infection prevention leads complete outbreak management training, including a scenario-based exercise, so the declaration and escalation steps above are familiar before a genuine outbreak makes them urgent.

Quality Lead review whether the control measures in place are genuinely working — for example, whether new cases keep appearing despite enhanced cleaning, which would suggest the transmission route has not been correctly identified — rather than mechanically continuing the same measures for the outbreak's full duration regardless of whether the case trend suggests they are having the intended effect.

Supporting residents' wellbeing during restricted communal activity

Where communal activities are restricted during an outbreak, the activities coordinator adapts the Activities and Wellbeing Programme Policy's own offer to smaller, in-room or cohort-specific activity rather than simply suspending meaningful engagement altogether for the outbreak's duration, since prolonged isolation carries its own genuine wellbeing cost that must be weighed against, not simply overridden by, the infection-control benefit of restriction.

Distinguishing an outbreak from a single, isolated infection

A single case of a transmissible infection, with no second case within the 48-hour window, is managed under everyday infection control practice rather than this procedure's outbreak-specific measures; the registered manager still monitors for a possible second case for a reasonable period afterward, but does not apply enhanced cleaning, cohorting or visiting restriction on the strength of one case alone, since doing so would impose the cost of an outbreak response without the actual outbreak having occurred.

Record of decisions, not only case counts

Beyond the daily case log, the registered manager keeps a brief, dated record of every significant decision made during an outbreak — when enhanced cleaning began, when cohorting was applied, when it was relaxed — since this decision log, not only the raw case numbers, is what a later review or regulatory enquiry actually needs to understand whether the response was timely and proportionate.

Coordinating with GP practices and community health services

Where an outbreak involves a condition requiring clinical input beyond Alderbridge's own staff (for example, confirming a diagnosis or advising on treatment for affected residents), the registered manager coordinates directly with the residents' own GP practices rather than each resident's care being managed in isolation from the wider outbreak response, ensuring clinical advice and Alderbridge's own infection-control measures are working from the same understanding of what is actually happening at the site.

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group prevents and responds to a slip, trip or fall hazard,

Emergency Preparedness Full Plan

following a sector-wide learning review, extending the plan's scope beyond single-site emergencies.

Purpose and scope

This plan sets out how Alderbridge Care Group prepares for, responds to, and recovers from a major
emergency affecting a site, now including a dedicated annex covering a pandemic or significant supply
chain disruption affecting the wider organisation rather than a single site alone. It applies to every site.

Policy statement

Alderbridge treats emergency preparedness as a continuous discipline; this version extends that discipline
to a sector-wide emergency, a pandemic or a significant supply chain disruption, that may affect every
Alderbridge site simultaneously rather than one site in isolation, requiring a different, organisation-wide
coordination approach to the single-site mutual aid model this plan already describes.

Definitions

**Major emergency** an incident causing significant disruption to safe care delivery. **Regional mutual
aid** the arrangement coordinating support between sites within a region. **Sector-wide emergency** the
new category, introduced in this version, covering a pandemic, a national supply chain disruption, or
another event affecting multiple or all Alderbridge sites simultaneously, requiring organisation-level rather
than purely regional or site-level coordination. **Critical supply** the new term, introduced in this version,
for an item, such as personal protective equipment or a specific medication category, whose unavailability
would directly compromise safe care.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds overall responsibility for their site's own emergency plan and now also
monitors local critical supply levels. **The regional manager** coordinates mutual aid within their region.
**The Health and Safety Lead**, in an expanded role introduced in this version, coordinates the
organisation-wide response to a sector-wide emergency, including critical supply allocation across regions,
and chairs the new organisation-level emergency coordination group for such an event.

Learning from Deaths Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group reviews a resident's death to identify any genuine learning, and how the family is communicated with. It applies to every site.

Policy statement

Every death is briefly reviewed at the next Quality Committee to identify any learning, without implying any death was unexpected or poorly managed, and every family is thanked for their trust and invited to share feedback.

Definitions

**Learning from deaths review** the brief, routine review conducted for every resident death, distinct from a fuller investigation triggered by a specific concern. **Quality Committee** the body that receives the review and any theme identified across multiple reviews over time.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** prepares a brief summary for the Quality Committee following every death. **The Quality Committee** identifies any genuine, recurring learning theme across reviews. **A nominated staff member** contacts the family sensitively to thank them and, where appropriate, invite feedback.

1. Prepare a brief review summary for every resident death, presented at the next Quality Committee meeting.
2. Identify whether the review suggests any genuine learning, distinct from the routine, expected nature of end of life care generally.
3. Contact the family, at a sensitive and appropriate time, to thank them for their trust in Alderbridge's care.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a death raises a specific concern beyond the routine review (for example, an unexpected circumstance), this is escalated to a fuller investigation under the Incident Reporting Policy and, where relevant, the Duty of Candour Guidance, rather than being addressed only through the routine Quality Committee review.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the Safer Recruitment Guidance (the same DBS standard applies), the Safe Administration of Medication Policy and Controlled Drugs Procedure (governing the medication restriction this version adds), and the Mandatory Training Matrix (defining which training an agency worker must hold before administering medication).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the new medication restriction in practice. An agency proposes a worker for a shift at Harbour View who holds a controlled drugs qualification from their home organisation. Under this version, that qualification alone is not sufficient — the worker administers only non-controlled medication until Alderbridge's own controlled drugs competency check is completed, illustrating that this version's new restriction applies regardless of an agency worker's genuine, verified experience elsewhere.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was verbal confirmation removed as an option?** A review found verbal-only bookings occasionally led to unclear expectations about which checks had actually been completed; requiring written confirmation for every booking closes that gap. **Can the same trusted agency worker cover multiple shifts without repeating checks each time?** Yes, provided their DBS and training status remain current and confirmed. **What if an urgent gap arises with no time to email a confirmation first?** The booking is still confirmed by email, even if sent slightly after a verbal agreement to proceed — the written record requirement is not waived, only its timing may be tightly compressed in a genuine emergency.

Training and competency

Shift leads booking agency staff complete brief training on the verification steps this policy requires, updated to reflect the written-confirmation and medication-restriction changes in this version.

Monitoring and compliance

Agency usage volume and any related incident or concern is reviewed quarterly by HR alongside the wider Mandatory Training Matrix compliance data, with specific attention to confirming the medication restriction is being applied consistently since its introduction.

Record keeping and retention

Agency booking and verification records, including the written confirmation this version requires, are retained per the Records Retention Schedule.

Approval and review history

This policy was originally approved by the Chief Executive on 1 January 2025 and this version took effect 1 February 2026, superseding the earlier version.

New and expectant mothers

A pregnant or breastfeeding employee's COSHH exposure is specifically reassessed as part of the wider

Extended worked example: a substance substitution decision

A worked example illustrates substitution as a genuine control measure, not just PPE as a first resort.
Following a staff concern about a strong-smelling floor cleaner at Harbour View, the Facilities Lead
reviews whether a lower-hazard alternative product achieves the same cleaning standard, trials one, and
switches the site's supply once satisfied it performs adequately — illustrating that COSHH control is not
simply about wearing the right PPE for a hazardous product, but about first asking whether a genuinely
less hazardous product could do the job at all, which is the higher-ranked control measure under the
regulations' own hierarchy.

Extended frequently asked questions

**What if I have a genuine allergy or sensitivity to a specific approved cleaning product?** Raise this with
the Facilities Lead, who arranges an alternative product for your use, recorded against your own file in the
same way as any other individual health-related workplace adjustment. **Are aerosols treated any
differently from liquid substances under COSHH?** Yes — aerosols carry their own specific inhalation and
flammability considerations noted on their SDS, and are stored away from any heat source specifically for
that reason. **Who do I ask if a product I use regularly doesn't seem to have an SDS on file?** Report this
to the Facilities Lead immediately and stop using the product until an SDS is obtained and reviewed, since
a substance without a current SDS on file has not actually been through the COSHH assessment process,
regardless of how long it may already have been in informal use.

This Statement of Purpose describes Alderbridge Care Group's service, in line with the requirement to
make this document available to residents, families and the Care Quality Commission. It applies to every
registered site.

Aims and objectives

Alderbridge provides high-quality residential and, at Harbour View, nursing care, supporting each resident
to live with dignity, independence and genuine choice.

Service type and registration

Alderbridge is registered to provide residential care for an older adult, including a resident living with
dementia, and Harbour View is additionally registered to provide nursing care.

Admission criteria

Admission is available to an adult, typically over 65, whose assessed needs can be safely met within a
residential care setting, or, at Harbour View, within a residential or nursing care setting.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates supervised access. An approved electrician attends to repair a fault in a
resident's room. Facilities confirms they are on the approved list, reception signs them in with a visitor
badge, and a member of staff remains present in the corridor throughout, checking in periodically rather
than leaving the contractor entirely unsupervised near a resident.

Frequently asked questions

booked and vetted attend; an additional person is checked and added to the booking first. **What happens
if a contractor's certification has expired since they were added to the approved list?** Facilities suspends
their approved status until it is renewed and verified.

site induction.

The approved contractor list is reviewed by facilities annually, confirming insurance and certification
remain current.
